To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) myasthenia is an autoimmune disease, (b) the thymus is the major target organ, (c) autoantibodies are directed against the acetylcholine receptor, (d) thymic abnormalities are present in the majority of patients with myasthennia, and (e) thymectomy improves the outcome of patients with generalized myasthenia.
the presence of anti-MuSK antibodies is associated with a younger age at onset of MG and a more severe disease, and the absence of anti-AChR antibodies.

the prevalence of anti-epithelial cell autoantibodies in the sera of patients with myasten gravis is higher than in the general population and that the autoantibodies are more common in patients who have had thymic surgery.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the immune system in myasthenic patients.
the study of autoimmunity in mya- sthenia gravis (MG) and in other autoimmune diseases.
the study of the role of autoimmunity and the role of thymic hormones in the pathogenesis of myasthenia.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
myasthenia is a disorder in which the patient has antibodies to acetylcholine receptor, and that these antibodies are directed against the alpha subunit of the acetylcholine receptors.
the autoantibodies found in myasthenic patients and their relatives are not specific for myasthenia, and that the autoantigen in myasthenics is not the muscle cell membrane.
the pathogenesis of MG is multifactorial and that the role of thymic abnormalities in the pathogenesis of the disease is not yet clear.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the prevalence of autoantbodies in the relatives of patients with myastehnia gravis is significantly higher than in the relatives of normal controls.

we have demonstrated that the autoantibodies in myasthenic sera are directed against a number of different antigens, that the autoantigens in myasthenics and nonmyasthenics are similar, that the auto-antibodies in patients with thymoma are similar to those in patients without thymoma, and that autoantibodies against acetylcholine receptor and against epithelial cells of the thymus are not related.
the autoimmunity is not limited to the thymus and the neuromuscular system.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the presence of these autoantibodies in the sera of patients with myasthena gravis and in their relatives is not random, but is associated with the presence of other autoantibodies.
the immune system can be trained to recognize the virus and attack it before it has the chance to do any damage.
the immune system is a complex network that is capable of producing antibodies to many different types of cells and molecules.
